article_title: Keeping New Teachers
citation: Lura Forcum and William Harms. (2005). New report shows that high-quality induction can help keep teachers on the job. University of Chicago press release announcing Keeping New Teachers: A First Look at the Influence of Induction in the Chicago Public Schools. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Provide high-quality induction combining mentoring, observation with feedback, guidance on rules and procedures, and classroom management support to keep new teachers
description: The article's central design recommendation is that new teachers receive high-quality induction rather than mere program participation. High-quality induction includes "mentoring activities such as observation of and feedback on their teaching; guidance with regard to CPS rules, policies, and procedures; and classroom management strategies." Novices receiving such induction are more likely to intend to continue teaching and report a good experience, and combined intensive mentoring and support shows the largest retention-plan differences.
requirements: Induction must include mentoring with observation of and feedback on teaching, guidance on district rules, policies, and procedures, and classroom management strategies.
Supports such as scheduled collaboration, teacher networks, release time to observe, and principal encouragement should accompany mentoring.
constraints: Participation in an induction program alone does not improve the chances teachers will remain; quality, not mere participation, is what matters.
The high school mentoring relationship was similar but not statistically significant.
target_learners: novice elementary and high school teachers in Chicago Public Schools, including career changers
target_learning_goals: teacher retention in the profession
a good early teaching experience
plans to remain in the same school
examples: The report compared novice teachers who received strong versus weak levels of mentoring and other supports on three outcomes: reporting a good experience, intending to continue teaching, and planning to remain in the same school.
key_sources: Lura Forcum and William Harms. (2005). New report shows that high-quality induction can help keep teachers on the job. University of Chicago press release announcing Keeping New Teachers: A First Look at the Influence of Induction in the Chicago Public Schools. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: High Dosage Tutoring for Academically At-Risk Students
citation: Davison, M., Postell, S., Isaacs, J., & Hashim, A. K. (2024). High dosage tutoring for academically at-risk students. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: High dosage tutoring implementation factor set: frequency and scheduling, group size, qualified personnel, outcome measurement, curriculum, tutor-to-student relationships, and removing barriers to access

These are "frequency and scheduling, group size, qualified personnel, measurement of outcomes, curriculum, tutor-to-student relationships, and new components like removing barriers to access." The set functions as a design checklist for schools or districts planning tutoring programs for at-risk students.
requirements: Implementation must attend to frequency and scheduling, group size, qualified personnel, measurement of outcomes, curriculum, and tutor-to-student relationships for the tutoring to work as described.
constraints: The brief notes that some components, such as removing barriers to access, are new additions to the factor set.
target_learners: Academically at-risk K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Accelerated academic growth in core academic subjects
examples: The brief reviews the research collection on high dosage tutoring and enumerates these factors as those that must be considered and included for effective implementation.

article_title: Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are
citation: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Hold high expectations for all learners so personalization advances equity rather than tracking
description: The paper argues personalized learning can advance equity only when paired with high expectations, contrasting it with traditional tracking that became permanent with different expectations and outcomes per group. It states that "Personalized learning has the potential to help advance equity in schools, as long as expectations are held high for all." To avoid permanent low tracks, personalized learning schools frequently remix performance groups, mixing academically homogeneous with heterogeneous groupings.
requirements: Clearly stated high expectations for everyone; equitable opportunities in the line of sight for all; remixing of performance groups rather than fixed tracks
constraints: Equity advocates worry about the shift of control back to states under ESSA; students most harmed by traditional systems include students of color, first-generation college students, economically disadvantaged students, and English language learners
target_learners: All students, particularly vulnerable groups harmed by traditional tracking
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to college- and career-ready outcomes
examples: Wilusz and Templeton's five elements of personalized learning that can lead to more equitable outcomes, including common standards for all students and choice in designing content, pathways, and products
key_sources: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org

article_title: A level playing field: College readiness standards
citation: Michael Dahlin and Beth Tarasawa. (2013). A Level Playing Field? How College Readiness Standards Change the Accountability Game. Northwest Evaluation Association. https://www.nwea.org
title: Recognize each school's top performers as an accountability subgroup when setting policy and evaluating school programs
description: The report recommends extending NCLB-style subgroup identification to high achievers, arguing each school has its own top tenth whose performance should affect the school's accountability score. It states we should "recognize the top performers in each school as a subgroup when setting accountability policy and evaluating school programs", so that schools attend to these students' needs just as they do for other subgroups. This leverages a mechanism the report credits with addressing achievement gaps.
requirements: State accountability systems must incorporate subgroup reporting so that each school's top performers are visible in evaluation
constraints: The report notes high achievers within a school may not be considered disadvantaged, so the case rests on compelling public interest rather than disadvantage mitigation
target_learners: high-achieving students in every school
minority and low-income high achievers
target_learning_goals: full academic potential of top performers
college readiness
examples: The foreword recommends policymakers reframe discussion to recognize that elite students should not be defined solely as the top 1%, 5%, or 10% of the standardized testing pool, since every school has its own group of elite students.

article_title: Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons from Innovative State Approaches under ESSA
citation: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper.
title: Hierarchy of Purposes of Statewide School Accountability Systems
description: The paper proposes a four-level hierarchical model of statewide school accountability systems, expanding on the National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment's four key roles. It argues that "the highest purpose of statewide school accountability systems should be to encourage specific action to improve school-level outcomes." The levels are cumulative: Level 1 identify purpose and vision; Level 2 design the system to serve that vision; Level 3 communicate accountability information to interest holders; Level 4 create linkages between accountability information and action, via horizontal coordination across the SEA and vertical coordination between SEA, districts, and schools.
requirements: States must identify the purpose and vision for the larger education system, often through strategic plans, theories of action, and logic models
Successfully implementing lower levels is necessary for the system to operate at higher levels
constraints: The model is proposed based on literature review and four case studies; the paper notes findings are not intended to be generalizable to all states
target_learners: state education agencies
district and school leaders
policymakers
target_learning_goals: connecting school accountability systems to school improvement and improved student outcomes
examples: The paper illustrates Level 4 with Mississippi's literacy gains, combining horizontal coordination across agencies through the Literacy-Based Promotion Act and vertical collaboration across all levels of the education system

article_title: Elementary School Principals' Professional Learning: Current Status and Future Needs
citation: Levin, S., Leung, M., Edgerton, A. K., & Scott, C. (2020). Elementary school principals’ professional learning: Current status and future needs. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/professional-learning-principals
title: Components of High-Quality Principal Professional Learning framework
description: The report proposes a conceptual framework (Figure 1) in which high-quality principal professional learning has two components: content and delivery. The content component “addresses” managing change, creating collegial environments, and improving instruction, the latter including whole child education and equitable opportunities. The delivery component “includes” applied learning, mentors or coaches, and network building. The framework derives from a 2017 LPI literature review identifying attributes of professional learning related to improved school outcomes, and it structures both the survey design and the report's policy recommendations.
requirements: Professional learning must pair relevant content topics with authentic, job-embedded delivery formats such as applied learning, mentoring or coaching, and PLCs
constraints: The report notes the literature on the impact of professional learning for principals is minimal, especially compared with the literature on teachers

Early-career and experienced school leaders
target_learning_goals: School leadership capacity
Leading schoolwide instructional improvement
Leading equitable schools and whole child education
examples: The NAESP-LPI survey measured principals' access to content topics and participation in applied learning, mentoring/coaching, and PLCs, mirroring the framework's two components

managing change

article_title: Educating for Equity: Alder Graduate School's Teacher Residency
citation: Yun, C., Fitz, J., Nakajima, T., & Mauerman, C. (2025). Educating for equity: Alder Graduate School's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/812.965
title: Alder's high-touch, whole adult support approach to resident success
description: The report describes Alder's organizing approach as a "high-touch, whole adult" model: recognizing that financial precarity and systemic inequities can block candidates' skill development, the program wraps residents in academic, financial, and social supports. An Office of Student Services proactively identified challenges "both through surveys and one-on-one conversations" and connected students with financial, food, housing, health care, academic, social, and hiring supports matched to need. The approach is framed as key to preparing the diverse educator pool Alder recruits.

constraints: Designed for a population whose financial precarity constitutes a potential barrier to accessing and completing a graduate-level degree

article_title: Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges
citation: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center
title: Five attributes of high-performing community colleges
description: The guide identifies attributes common to high-performing colleges that support completion pathways: learning- and outcomes-focused leadership in which faculty, staff, administrators, and trustees make student learning and completion their top priorities; student-centered change that gathers information about student experiences and engages students in developing reforms; a culture of improvement and use of data examining loss and momentum points and costs; faculty engagement and professional development built into organizational and reward structures, including incentives for adjunct faculty; and technology capacity to increase effectiveness and efficiency of service and instructional delivery. All attributes, the guide notes, require teamwork across roles and functions since they are directed toward system integration.

target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes and completion rates
examples: Example attributes in action include collegewide Pathways Analysis teams, structured peer mentoring among full-time and adjunct faculty, and hybrid or blended formats in large entry-level courses

Gradual taking on of teaching responsibility under mentor guidance

article_title: State Guidance for High-Impact Tutoring
citation: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://studentsupportaccelerator.org
title: Research-based guardrails for high-impact tutoring programs: school-day scheduling, at least three sessions weekly, consistent tutors, tutor training and coaching, data use, and aligned materials

article_title: From Traditional Classroom to AI-Enhanced Flipped Classroom: A Three-Year Pedagogical Evolution for International Students in Pharmacology
citation: Liu YJ, Ma HZ, Luo HY, Xiong YX, Qu FW, Xie JP, Guo Y. (2026). From traditional classroom to AI-enhanced flipped classroom: a three-year pedagogical evolution for international students in pharmacology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09608-7
title: HI-AI collaborative flipped classroom framework explained by constructivist learning theory, cognitive load theory, and the technology acceptance model
description: The article proposes a human intelligence (HI)-AI collaborative framework layered on the flipped classroom, in which AI provides "real-time information resources and support for instructional process analysis" while teachers design higher-order tasks and give in-depth feedback. Three complementary theoretical perspectives explain the observed patterns: constructivist learning theory, cognitive load theory, and the technology acceptance model (TAM). AI is positioned as a cognitive scaffold that reduces extraneous load and frees resources for instructor-led higher-order activities.

Instructor guidance rules requiring students to verify and rewrite AI outputs
constraints: Benefits may not be replicable in resource-limited settings where such tools are unavailable
In teacher-centred systems or contexts discouraging AI reliance, implementation requires tailored adaptation and faculty development
Tested only in a single pharmacology course with international students from South and Southeast Asia
target_learners: third-year international undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: pharmacological knowledge integration and clinical decision-making
higher-order clinical thinking
self-directed learning
examples: In the 2025 cohort, students used DeepSeek V3.1 and Kimi for information gathering, outline generation, and concept explanation across all three course phases, with AI also supporting instructional process analysis in class.

article_title: Automating Constructive Assessment with Large Language Models: Toward Scalable and Repeated Evaluation of Practical Competence
citation: Satoshi Takahashi, Atsushi Yoshikawa, Megumi Kose, Kenichi Suzuki, Chieko Inoue, Yumi Watanabe, and Mari Sawada. (2026). Automating Constructive Assessment with Large Language Models: Toward Scalable and Repeated Evaluation of Practical Competence. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25790
title: Hierarchical Diagnostic Reasoning (HDR): a structured constructive assessment of practical judgment
description: HDR is a descriptive assessment proposed by Takahashi et al. (2025) that "diagnoses learners' applied cognitive skills through practical cases containing the misuse of knowledge." It conceptualizes reasoning hierarchically: (1) read and understand the scenario, (2) identify the error, and (3) explain why it is incorrect. Each question combines error selection with a rationale description in a pre-defined frame, so responses converge and the learner's practical judgment and structural understanding are visualized. This study automates the full HDR cycle—problem generation, scoring, and feedback—using ChatGPT prompt design.
requirements: Problems must embed intentional misuses of knowledge aligned with educational intentions, which traditionally requires specialized expertise
Scoring requires unified judgment criteria given to learners (e.g., target only descriptions containing errors; judge based on information within the case)
constraints: Designing problems with intentionally misused knowledge requires specialized expertise
Scoring descriptive answers and creating individual feedback traditionally depend on human resources, making large-scale implementation and immediacy difficult
target_learners: Working adults in business/MBA education
target_learning_goals: Practical judgment and structural understanding of applied knowledge (e.g., STP analysis)
Higher-order cognitive skills such as analysis and evaluation
examples: The original problem was a seven-paragraph STP case study about an electronics manufacturer's sales representative, with three embedded errors identified through interviews with business-education practitioners

article_title: Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact
citation: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883
title: A four-step methodological framework for measuring LLM alignment to intended impact in high-noise contexts
description: The article proposes a general framework for evaluating whether LLM judgments align with real-world outcomes when experimental control is infeasible. It comprises (1) correlating behaviors across the space of generalization with dCor2n dependence measures, (2) measuring best-proxy alignment on downstream tasks using Kendall's tau, described as "a simple, strong option that can be estimated with any datatype", (3) establishing real-world baselines such as teacher experience or prior VAM, and (4) decomposing misalignment error variance via Generalizability Theory. It was applied to classroom-transcript scoring against expert ratings and value-added measures.
requirements: requires external criteria representing both the downstream task and the intended impact of that task, however noisy
constraints: intended-impact data may be time-delayed after the downstream tasks or have grain-size mismatches, requiring real-world baselines for comparison
target_learners: schoolchildren in evaluated classrooms
target_learning_goals: student academic growth as measured by value-added achievement gains
examples: Applied to 16 LLMs rating 479 primary mathematics lesson transcripts across seven tasks, with alignment measured against MQI/CLASS expert ratings and stacked value-added measures
key_sources: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883

article_title: Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues
citation: Zhangqi Duan, Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan. (2026). Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30051
title: History-conditioned student simulation: two-component profile-generator-plus-simulator framework
description: The article establishes the task of history-conditioned student simulation, where a model predicts a student's next tutoring-dialogue turn conditioned on their prior question-answering and dialogue history. "We propose a two-component framework in which a profile generator summarizes a student's history and a simulator predicts student turns conditioned on the resulting profile." Both components are trained with reinforcement learning so that profiles are optimized for faithful downstream simulation: the simulator is fine-tuned with SFT then DPO against counterfactual mismatched profiles, and the profile generator is distilled then refined with GRPO using ground-truth turn log-likelihood as reward.
requirements: Student learning histories containing both question-answering records and tutoring dialogues
A compact profile representation because directly conditioning on full histories is often infeasible
constraints: Histories are trimmed heuristically to the most recent 8 QA interactions and 3 dialogues due to context-length and memory limitations
target_learners: Math students practicing on online learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Faithful simulation of student knowledge state and dialogue behavior for tutor evaluation and training
examples: The framework was instantiated as ProfileRL with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct base models trained via LoRA and evaluated on the math platform dataset

article_title: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for AI-Assisted Scoring in Large-Scale Writing Assessment
citation: Curi, M. E., Capdehourat, G., Amigo, I., Romano, M., Serra, R., Silveira, A., Peri, A. (2026). A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for AI-Assisted Scoring in Large-Scale Writing Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05143
title: Human-in-the-Loop AI-assisted evaluation framework for high-stakes writing assessment
description: A decision-oriented operational framework integrating LLM-based scoring of the Writing section into a national exam workflow while keeping humans in charge of outcome-determining decisions. Its central principle is "ensuring that no final decision affecting test outcomes is made without appropriate human oversight." The workflow (Fig. 8) runs a calibration phase (50–100 texts) to validate the AI model and adapt prompts, scores all responses automatically, applies IRT and Bookmark cut scores, reviews candidates whose pass/fail outcome depends on the Writing section, and recalibrates cut scores after review. Other test sections remain scored by current operational procedures.
requirements: A calibration phase (50–100 texts) to validate the AI model and adapt prompts to the current test topic; IRT and Bookmark cut-score procedures to assign proficiency levels before routing decisions.
constraints: The study was conducted under offline experimental conditions, and operational deployment may surface additional challenges related to monitoring, drift, and edge cases; the workload reduction varies across editions depending on candidate performance in other test sections.
target_learners: Over-age adults (21+) seeking lower secondary education certification in Uruguay's national Acredita EB assessment

citation: Youqing Fang, Yinhao Tang, Yanan Sun, Jiangning Liu, Ziyi Wang, Xun Zhao, Bin Liu, Weiming Zhang, Kuikun Liu, Wenwei Zhang, Kai Chen. (2026). MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23535
title: Human-in-the-Loop MDP formulation of co-writing
description: The article models interactive co-writing as a sequential decision process in which the assistant proposes context-aware suggestions and the human author responds with accept, reject, or edit actions that update the document state. It states: "We model this iterative process as a Human-in-the-Loop Markov Decision Process (HitL-MDP), which makes explicit the division of roles between proposing and deciding." The formulation defines the process as M=<S,A,U,T> with transitions enacted through human actions, and grounds learning and evaluation in observable human responses to system proposals.
requirements: Suggestions must be non-binding, with all document updates determined by the human author, so that acceptance and editing behavior is observable.
constraints: The framework targets suggestion-based interactive completion, an abstraction of real-world authoring; generalization to other collaborative forms such as outlining assistance or structural critiquing remains an open question.

target_learning_goals: sustaining writing flow and author intent alignment during human-AI co-writing

article_title: Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition
citation: Paritosh Parmar, Landy Lan, Hong Yang, Chen Yi, Chiat Pin Tay. (2026). Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05115
title: Hierarchical multi-order kinematic representation with multi-objective knowledge distillation framework
description: A motion-reasoning framework in which human actions are represented as a hierarchy of kinematic orders: "we represent motion using joint positions, velocities, and accelerations, which are later encoded by dedicated order-specific backbones." Order-specific representations are fused by weighted averaging into a multi-order teacher, which is distilled via a multi-objective loss (temperature-scaled KL distillation plus supervised classification) into a substantially smaller student operating only on zeroth-order joint positions. The design compresses along two axes: from multi-order inputs to a single zeroth-order stream, and from a larger teacher network to a smaller student.
requirements: Temporal preprocessing before computing derivatives, since higher-order kinematic features amplify errors present in lower-order pose estimates; missing joints are linearly interpolated and trajectories smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter
constraints: In the implementation the fusion weights are set manually
The deployed student operates only on a single zeroth-order joint-position stream at inference
target_learners: preschool students and teachers in monitored classrooms
target_learning_goals: privacy-preserving recognition of classroom safety incidents from pose sequences alone
examples: Instantiated with STGCN++ backbones: 64-base-channel order-specific teachers and a 32-channel student, with distillation temperature 4 and loss weights {λKD, λCls} = {0.3, 1.0}

article_title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
citation: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, and Dora Demszky. (2025). Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise. arXiv:2410.03017v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03017v2
title: Taxonomy of high-quality strategies that foster understanding versus low-quality strategies that lead students to the solution
description: The article defines a two-category taxonomy of tutor moves in mathematics tutoring, drawing on prior work. High-quality strategies "foster students' understanding": prompting the student to explain, asking questions to guide thinking, and affirming the student's correct attempt. Low-quality strategies "lead students directly to the solution or passively engage students": asking the student to retry, giving away the answer/explanation, giving away the solution strategy, and encouraging the student in a generic way. Binary RoBERTa classifiers identified these strategies at scale with F1-scores between 0.65 and 0.90.

constraints: Developed for K-12 mathematics tutoring chat interactions

target_learning_goals: Deeper conceptual understanding of mathematics rather than task completion

citation: Nicola Brocca, Davide Garassino. (2026). LLMs in text linguistics teaching: an exploratory study with genAI novices in higher education. Computers and Education Open 11 (2026) 100414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100414
title: Human-in-the-loop LLM workflow as a metacognitive framework for AI-assisted learning
description: The article conceptualizes LLM integration in learning through a Human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow in which learners alternate between manual analysis, prompting, evaluating model outputs, and refining prompts. The authors state that "This interaction between human and machine reflects a metacognitive process, in which users continuously monitor the adequacy of the LLM's output and adjust their strategies accordingly". In the study, this framework grounded the deductive coding of student prompts and underpins the conclusion that prompting and output evaluation are metacognitive practices. article_title: Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology
citation: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105
title: Highly structured course design: daily and weekly active-learning exercises with frequent low-stakes formative assessment
description: The highly structured course design assigns "daily and weekly active-learning exercises with the goal of providing constant practice with the analytical skills required to do well on exams," in contrast to low-structure courses based on lecturing and two or three midterms plus a comprehensive final. Its components, added in implementation order, were clicker questions in peer-instruction format, weekly online peer-graded practice exams, open-book reading quizzes on basic vocabulary and concepts, class notes summaries aimed at metacognition, and in-class group exercises with random-call participation replacing Socratic lecturing. Moderate structure added clickers and practice exams; high structure added reading quizzes and group exercises.
requirements: Requires frequent low-stakes assessment points (clicker questions, practice exams, reading quizzes) that together represent a minority of total course points, with exams remaining the primary determinant of grade
constraints: The study population was sophomores who had completed a chemistry prerequisite, so failure rates were lower than at many other institutions before any intervention
target_learners: Undergraduate biology majors in large introductory gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Higher-order cognitive skills at the application and analysis levels of Bloom's taxonomy, and reduced course failure
examples: In Autumn 2007 and Autumn 2009 quarters, class sessions consisted of a series of 3- to 5-min mini-lectures around clicker questions or group exercises, with five or six group exercises per session and 12–15 students called on each day

citation: Arán Filippetti, Vanessa; Krumm, Gabriela Liliana (2020). A hierarchical model of cognitive flexibility in children: Extending the relationship between flexibility, creativity and academic achievement. Child Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2019.1711034

description: The article proposes a hierarchical account in which cognitive flexibility comprises two related components: reactive flexibility and spontaneous flexibility. Spontaneous flexibility is characterized as "the ability to generate diverse responses driven by internal stimuli," and the authors raise "the question whether considering SF as a higher-level form of cognitive flexibility (different from a lower-level shifting skill) could be an interesting approach for the study of cognitive flexibility in children." The model is grounded in the two-factor CFA solution and the differential executive and academic-creativity correlates reported in the two studies.

constraints: The hierarchical framing is raised as an open question for future study rather than asserted as an established finding

target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility
creative divergent response generation
reading comprehension
writing

These parameters become more complexly integrated with age, and the authors distinguish an apprentice stage of culture-driven control over identity from a master stage of personally defined control over productivity.

article_title: Alternate reality gaming and convergence culture
citation: Henrik Örnebring. (2007). Alternate reality gaming and convergence culture: The case of Alias. International Journal of Cultural Studies 10(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/1367877907083079
title: Hierarchy-of-meaning critique of convergence culture: an identifiable ur-text marketed through secondary texts
description: The article proposes a corrective to Jenkins' convergence culture concept. Rather than convergence dissolving text boundaries into decentralized trans-media narratives, it argues convergence creates new opportunities to market a specific text through other texts, with a 'hierarchy of meaning' among texts and a clearly identifiable ur-text (the Alias TV series) marketed through books, comics and ARGs. Reverse flows, where the TV series takes up threads from other media texts, are described as much rarer.

constraints: The account is developed from analysis of ARGs tied to one TV franchise; the article notes industry ARGs based on existing properties are often more circumscribed and redundant than Jenkins would care to admit.

citation: Dovis, S., Van der Oord, S., Wiers, R.W., & Prins, P.J.M. (2015). ADHD subtype differences in reinforcement sensitivity and visuospatial working memory. Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, 44(5), 859-874. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2014.895940
title: Use high reinforcement to improve visuospatial STM and WM performance in children with ADHD
description: The article shows that raising reinforcement above a standard feedback-only level improves visuospatial STM and WM performance in children with ADHD. In the experiment, a high level of reinforcement was operationalized as "feedback + 10 euros" on top of standard feedback. The improvement occurred in both the ADHD-C and ADHD-I subtypes and was "equally pronounced in both subtypes", supporting reinforcement as a motivational lever for these children. The principle applies specifically to STM and WM tasks, not to CE-related performance.

target_learning_goals: visuospatial working memory
visuospatial short-term memory
examples: The experiment compared a standard feedback-only condition with a high-reinforcement condition of feedback + 10 euros in children aged 9-12 with ADHD-I, ADHD-C, and controls.

article_title: Differential effects of socioeconomic status on working and procedural memory systems
citation: Leonard JA, Mackey AP, Finn AS and Gabrieli JDE (2015) Differential effects of socioeconomic status on working and procedural memory systems. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 9:554. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2015.00554
title: Dissociated multiple memory systems: hippocampal-prefrontal declarative/working memory vs. striatal procedural memory
description: The article's organizing framework is a fundamental dissociation between two memory systems with separable neural substrates. Complex working memory and declarative memory "appears to depend upon the integrity of a memory system that involves both MTL and DLPFC regions," whereas procedural memory, "measured implicitly by skill learning over time, does not depend upon the MTL structures supporting declarative and complex working memory, but rather depends upon the integrity of the basal ganglia." The probabilistic classification task is the behavioral probe of the striatal system, with amnesic patients showing intact learning and Parkinson's patients impaired learning. The study uses this framework to predict and interpret SES's selective effects.
requirements: The framework rests on convergent lesion and neuroimaging evidence in humans and animals distinguishing MTL/DLPFC-dependent from basal-ganglia-dependent learning
constraints: The article notes the systems interact: the striatum plays a role in working memory, and probabilistic learning engages both MTL and striatal systems in different ways depending on feedback-based versus paired-association learning
target_learners: adolescents from lower- and higher-SES backgrounds
target_learning_goals: working memory capacity
procedural (implicit) skill learning such as probabilistic classification
examples: The study measured count span (working memory) and probabilistic classification (procedural memory) alongside hippocampal, DLPFC, and caudate volumes in the same adolescents.

article_title: Hippocampal-neocortical functional reorganization underlies children's cognitive development
citation: Qin Shaozheng, Cho Soohyun, Chen Tianwen, Rosenberg-Lee Miriam, Geary David C., Menon Vinod. (2014). Hippocampal-neocortical functional reorganization underlies children's cognitive development. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.3788
title: Hippocampal-neocortical consolidation account of the development of memory-based problem solving
description: The article advances an account in which the hippocampus plays a time-limited role in the early phase of academic knowledge acquisition, fostering rapid binding of new information that is gradually consolidated into neocortical representations. The authors write that "the hippocampus plays a critical, but time-limited, role in the early phase of knowledge acquisition, and this hippocampal dependence is reduced following reconfiguration of neocortical connections and stabilization of newly acquired knowledge – a process referred to as consolidation." Their longitudinal and cross-sectional findings — rising then falling hippocampal engagement, connectivity-predicted retrieval gains, and increasing representational stability — are presented as support for this consolidation framework in children's arithmetic learning.

transition from procedure-based to memory-based problem solving

title: Design teacher professional development around content focus, active learning, collaboration, modelling, coaching, feedback and sustained duration
description: The article grounds iSELF's instructional practices in research on effective teacher professional development. Citing a review of 35 PDPs, it lists characteristics of effective programs: they "incorporate active learning, (3) support teacher collaboration, (4) use models and modelling, (5) offer coaching and expert support, (6) stimulate feedback and reflection and (7) are of sustained duration". Table 2 shows how each iSELF session enacted these characteristics, on the premise that teachers engage more when participation benefits their own and their students' development.
requirements: professional development should combine content focus with active learning, collaboration, modelling, coaching, feedback and reflection over a sustained period
target_learners: primary education teachers
target_learning_goals: teachers' ability to provide explicit SRL instruction
examples: iSELF's plenary training and three coaching sessions were each mapped onto the enacted characteristics in Table 2, with in-between assignments such as processing materials and preparing observed lessons

article_title: Effects of innovative science and mathematics teaching on student attitudes and achievement: A meta-analytic study
citation: Savelsbergh, E. R., Prins, G. T., Rietbergen, C., Fechner, S., Vaessen, B. E., Draijer, J. M., & Bakker, A. (2016). Effects of innovative science and mathematics teaching on student attitudes and achievement: A meta-analytic study. Educational Research Review, 19, 158-172. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2016.07.003
title: Hierarchical framework of domain-specific attitude constructs for synthesizing attitude outcomes
description: The article proposes a hierarchical conceptual framework (Fig. 1) for classifying attitude measures at multiple grain sizes, balancing fine-grained and global analyses. The authors "consider attitude a multidimensional construct comprising: perceived relevance (personal and societal), interest (school, leisure, career), self-efficacy, and normality of scientists", with an overall attitude construct for aggregated measures. It was used to categorize attitude instruments across the 65 experiments and to justify separate meta-analyses for specific and global outcomes.
requirements: Attitude instruments must assess domain-specific attitudes and be validated or report reliability statistics and at least three sample items per scale
constraints: Scientific attitudes (critical stance, demand for verification) fall beyond the framework's scope as applied in this review
target_learners: primary and secondary students in science and mathematics education
target_learning_goals: domain-specific attitudes, interest, and motivation toward science and mathematics
examples: The framework sorted the 65 experiments' attitude measures into subscales such as general interest, career interest, self-efficacy, and normality of scientist, each meta-analyzed separately (Table 4).

article_title: Scaffolding what, why and how? A critical thematic review study of descriptions, goals, and means of language scaffolding in Bilingual education contexts
citation: Ertugruloglu, E.O.; Mearns, T.L.; Admiraal, W.F. (2023). Scaffolding what, why and how? A critical thematic review study of descriptions, goals, and means of language scaffolding in Bilingual education contexts. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100550
title: Hierarchy of language scaffolding goals: focusing on disciplinary literacy presupposes a focus on content and language
description: The review proposes an organizing account of language scaffolding goals in bilingual secondary education in which the goals form a hierarchy rather than a flat set. Within this hierarchy, "focusing on disciplinary literacy presupposes a focus on content and language", meaning that pursuing disciplinary literacy as a scaffolding goal builds on, and depends on, prior attention to content and language. The hierarchy emerged from the review's thematic synthesis of the four identified scaffolding goals.
requirements: Applies to language scaffolding by subject teachers in bilingual secondary education contexts
target_learners: secondary school students in bilingual education learning content through a partially known language
target_learning_goals: disciplinary literacy
content learning
language learning
examples: The review synthesizes studies of subject teachers teaching in bilingual secondary education contexts and orders their scaffolding goals into this hierarchy.

article_title: Historical Reasoning: Towards a Framework for Analyzing Students’ Reasoning about the Past
citation: Jannet van Drie & Carla van Boxtel. (2008). Historical Reasoning: Towards a Framework for Analyzing Students' Reasoning about the Past. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9056-1
title: Six-component framework of historical reasoning
description: The article defines historical reasoning as "an activity in which a person organizes information about the past in order to describe, compare, and/or explain historical phenomena". The framework comprises six analytically separable but interrelated components: asking historical questions, using sources, contextualization, argumentation, using substantive concepts, and using meta-concepts. It was developed and refined through coding student essays, chat discussions, small-group and whole-class discussions, and is intended to describe progression and task effects in secondary history education.
requirements: Quality of reasoning can only be judged relative to the nature of the task, the topic or theme, the historical materials, and the background knowledge expected of the student
constraints: The components are analytical tools and do not occur clearly separated in reality; the framework defines no fixed categories of high and low level historical reasoning
target_learners: secondary education students
target_learning_goals: historical reasoning: describing, comparing, and explaining historical phenomena
examples: The authors used the framework's coding schemes to identify differences in the amount and quality of historical reasoning between tasks and between experts and novices in various studies

article_title: Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships
citation: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y
title: Hierarchical structure of teachers' mental relationship representations at global, domain-specific, and relationship-specific levels
description: Drawing on attachment theory, the review proposes that teachers internalize relationship experiences into mental representations at "different levels of generalization": a global interpersonal orientation, domain-specific models of relationships with students containing beliefs about teaching roles and self-efficacy, and relationship-specific models for individual children containing "a teacher's image of the child, a sense of her- or himself in interaction with the child as well as internalized feelings." The relationship-specific models are nested within the domain-specific model, which is nested in the global model, explaining how individual relationships can affect teachers' professional and personal self-esteem.
requirements: Physical proximity between teachers and students is believed to trigger the development of domain-specific and relationship-specific models
constraints: The review states it is aware of no studies that have tested whether teachers construct relationship models at different levels of generalization
target_learners: teachers in preschool through upper elementary education
target_learning_goals: understanding teacher emotional responses to individual students
teacher self-esteem and wellbeing

article_title: Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation
citation: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7
title: Hierarchical model of achievement motivation: energization and direction as separate, hierarchically linked components
description: The hierarchical model of achievement motivation is an integrative framework in which energization and direction are separate, equally important components of motivation. Energization is the 'why' of behavior and exerts a distal, indirect influence, while direction channels it into concrete goal pursuit that proximally predicts behavior. The model is hierarchical in focus (abstract-to-concrete constructs) and function (energizing vs. guiding roles), and the authors present it as 'a theoretical foundation from which integrative work may be organized and carried out.'
requirements: Constructs must be precisely defined and conceptualized so their nature and boundaries are clearly understood before integration
constraints: The model requires competence to be present in either the energization or the direction component for achievement motivation to be implicated
target_learners: students in achievement contexts
learners across school, sport, and work domains
target_learning_goals: competence-relevant behavior and achievement outcomes
examples: The model links achievement motives (energization) to achievement goals (direction), which in turn proximally predict intrinsic motivation and academic performance
key_sources: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7

article_title: Involving the Body to Improve Letter Knowledge and Script: an Experimental Study in French Kindergarten
citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Natacha Boissicat, Fanny Gimbert, Céline Pobel-Burtin, Marie-Caroline Croset, Marie-Line Bosse, and Cécile Nurra. (2024). Involving the Body to Improve Letter Knowledge and Script: An Experimental Study in French Kindergarten. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09923-9
title: Hierarchical memory-trace framework for sensorimotor training design
description: The article proposes that bodily experiences be organized by the proximity of their memory traces to the learning content: specific (pencil-and-paper), intermediate (arm), and general (body) levels. It assumes "memory traces generated by bodily experiences more distal to the content of the activity" need to be "nested within memory traces of more proximal levels" to create synergies in learning. Training conditions are nested: arm training combines specific and intermediate traces, arm-body training all three levels. The framework draws on embodied cognition, the modality-like "multimodality effect", the variability effect, and the human movement effect from cognitive load theory.
requirements: Higher-level bodily movement training must be combined with lower-level training (e.g., handwriting exercises in all conditions) so that distal memory traces are nested within proximal ones
constraints: A pilot study without handwriting exercises in the arm and arm-body conditions showed null or negative effects of bodily engagement, which the authors attributed to the lack of specific sensorimotor experiences
target_learners: Kindergarten students (around 5 years old) acquiring pre-reading skills
target_learning_goals: Letter knowledge (letter recognition, letter-name knowledge)
Letter script skills (dictation, stroke direction, legibility)
examples: The experiment nested conditions: pencil-and-paper training allocated 100% of time to writing activity traces; arm training allocated 45% to handwriting and 55% to arm tracing; arm-body training allocated 45% handwriting, 11% arm, 44% body training

article_title: Effects of 8 Weeks with Embodied Learning on 5–6-Year-Old Danish Children’s Pre-reading Skills and Word Reading Skills: the PLAYMORE Project, DK
citation: Linn Damsgaard, Anne-Mette Veber Nielsen, Anne Kær Gejl, Anne Sofie Bøgh Malling, Søren Kildahl Jensen, Jacob Wienecke. (2022). Effects of 8 Weeks with Embodied Learning on 5–6-Year-Old Danish Children's Pre-reading Skills and Word Reading Skills: the PLAYMORE Project, DK. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1709–1737. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09671-8
title: Use high bodily engagement with high task integration as a supplement to handwriting when teaching letter-sound associations
description: The authors recommend that letter-sound instruction combine movements closely integrated with the learning content, since their intervention groups with "high bodily engagement and high task integration" outperformed a handwriting-only control on letter-sound knowledge. The recommendation is explicitly positioned as a supplement to, not a replacement for, handwriting.
requirements: Movements must be meaningfully and congruently coupled to the letter-sounds being learned, performed while pronouncing the sound
constraints: Benefit was shown for letter-sound knowledge, not word reading; the control group still involved handwriting and hearing, described as a lesser degree of embodiment
target_learners: 5–6-year-old children beginning formal reading instruction (grade 0)
target_learning_goals: Letter-sound knowledge, including standard and conditional pronunciations
examples: Children in WM stood in a circle making whole-body phoneme movements left to right while pronouncing sounds; HM children made arm-and-hand movements seated; CON children did seated pencil-and-paper activities

title: Give higher priority to teaching children to use their first or main language effectively across social contexts, supported by robust oracy assessment
description: The article argues that teaching children how to use their first or main language effectively across a range of social contexts should be given higher priority 'in educational policy and school practice'. It further argues that developing robust, practicable ways of assessing oracy will help achieve that goal, and the Toolkit was developed partly to serve this aim.

target_learning_goals: using spoken language effectively across a range of social contexts
examples: The Cambridge Oracy Assessment Toolkit was developed as a research-informed resource for assessing oracy, intended to help give oracy higher priority in policy and school practice

article_title: Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning
citation: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141
title: Implement adaptive teaching with high fidelity: apply adaptive elements constantly, since benefits emerge only in highly adaptive units
description: The article's central practical recommendation is that adaptive teaching pays off only when implemented with many adaptive elements. As the authors put it, "teachers need to carefully apply adaptive elements constantly, since our results demonstrated that adaptive teaching units were only more effective than regular teaching when the degree of adaptivity was high." Degree of adaptivity was measured as the number of formative assessments, macro- and micro-level adaptations, and consolidation phases implemented per unit. Units above the sample mean of adaptive elements outperformed control classes; units below it did not.
requirements: Frequent formative assessments and tailored instructional supports across the four levels: formative assessments, macro- and micro-level adaptations, and consolidation phases
Professional development and research-team support so digital tools support rather than dictate adaptivity
constraints: The 18-element cut-off was derived from the conditions' mean degree of adaptivity, not tested as an optimum
Benefits in STEM and humanities were not significant, so high adaptivity alone may not suffice in every domain
target_learners: secondary school students in grades 7-12
target_learning_goals: lasting subject-matter knowledge and self-efficacy in using technology
examples: Teachers in the study co-designed units over two to three months in tandems with workshops and feedback sessions, integrating online quizzes, group-work platforms, and automated feedback systems
key_sources: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141

article_title: The Rôle of the Teacher in the Most Expeditious and Economic Learning.
citation: Book, William Frederick. (1908). The Role of the Teacher in the Most Expeditious and Economic Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+Role+of+the+Teacher+in+the+Most+Expeditious+and+Economic+Learning
title: Hierarchy-of-habits account: skills form as hierarchies of manipulation and control habits in which elemental and higher-order habits develop together
description: Book describes skill acquisition as the formation of two groups of habits: "habits of manipulation, a complicated hierarchy of psycho-physical habits having to do with the writing as such, and (b) habits of control," the latter characterized as learning to learn. Elemental associations are adapted from old familiar activities, selected and eliminated into letter associations, then short-circuited into word habits and higher complexes. Crucially, the levels develop together: "the lower-order habits are perfected in and through the formation of the higher even as the further development of the higher is dependent upon the perfection of the lower." The teacher's role is to see this natural method followed rather than an artificial, logical one.
requirements: Elemental habits must be thoroughly learned and perfected before higher-order habits can safely be built on them
Practice with the highest-order habits possible so all units are learned in their proper setting
constraints: The account is drawn from studies of acquisition such as typewriting and telegraphy; the most economic periods of work and rest in different fields still required further investigation
target_learners: Learners acquiring complex skills such as typewriting or telegraphy
target_learning_goals: Formation and progressive organization of skill habits
Learning to learn, i.e., habits of control
examples: The typewriting learners' first circuitous writing methods were simplified and reorganized into direct letter associations, then into word habits and higher complexes

article_title: Hierarchical nature of arithmetic skills: Similarities and differences between arithmetic operations.
citation: Rautiainen, J., Aro, T., Aro, M., Tolvanen, A., & Koponen, T. (2026). Hierarchical Nature of Arithmetic Skills: Similarities and Differences Between Arithmetic Operations. Journal of Educational Psychology, Early online. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001066
title: Hierarchical development framework of arithmetic operations with operation-specific cognitive architectures
description: The article frames arithmetic skill development as hierarchical: prior operations contribute greatly to subsequent ones (subtraction is the inverse of addition, multiplication is repeated addition), while each operation retains a partially distinct cognitive architecture of numerical and non-numerical precursors. The article states that "Arithmetic development is suggested to be hierarchical in the sense that prior skills contribute greatly to subsequent skills." The study operationalizes this by modeling how fall-of-second-grade numerical abilities, serial retrieval fluency, and working memory predict third-grade multiplication fluency, with addition, subtraction, or reading fluency as hierarchically positioned lower skills whose covariance is partialled out via specific factors.
requirements: Requires longitudinal measurement of both hierarchically lower skills (addition, subtraction fluency in spring of second grade) and the target skill (multiplication fluency in spring of third grade)
constraints: The article notes the interrelatedness of operations may partly stem from educational practices rather than shared cognitive architecture
Findings are situated in the Finnish instructional context; instructional and curricular approaches were not examined in the study
target_learners: primary school children in grades 1-3
target_learning_goals: arithmetic fluency development across addition, subtraction, and multiplication
examples: The study modeled 207 children across five assessment points from first to third grade using structural equation modeling with hierarchically lower skills captured in specific factors (F1)

citation: Rugg, E. (1921). New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Four methods of presenting history subject matter: textbook, source, topical, and problem methods
description: The review reports that Tryon's book, from the point of view of educational method, discusses the history recitation and, in that connection, presents a set of distinct methods for delivering history subject matter. As printed, "the textbook, source, topical and problem methods" are the named alternatives the book treats. The reviewer presents this as a distinguishing feature of the book's treatment of educational method.
requirements: The methods are described as approaches to presenting subject matter within the history recitation, as treated in the reviewed book.

article_title: A New Book for Teachers of History.
citation: Rugg, E. (1921). New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: History teaching books should treat the psychological processes involved in learning history, including imagination and judgment
description: The reviewer regrets that the author did not discuss more in detail psychological and pedagogical phases of history teaching. He names as important questions of educational method "the use of imagination and judgment are important questions of educational method with which any history teacher should be familiar," alongside association and the repetition needed to fix connections. article_title: Recent publications in history [Four articles and two books].
citation: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: History examinations should test interpretation and use of historical materials rather than memoriter reproduction of isolated facts
description: In his chapter on the history examination, Johnson, as reported by the reviewer, "deplores the emphasis placed upon the memoriter reproduction of isolated historical facts, and urges a type of examination which will show the pupils' ability to interpret and utilize historical materials, situations or generalizations." The principle holds that assessment in history should reveal whether pupils can work with historical content, not merely recall it. The reviewer presents this as Johnson's central recommendation for examination practice.
requirements: Examination tasks built around historical materials, situations or generalizations that pupils must interpret and utilize

article_title: Using social and behavioral science to address achievement inequality
citation: Brummelman, E., van Atteveldt, N., Wolf, S. & Sierksma, J. (2024). Using social and behavioral science to address achievement inequality. npj Science of Learning, 9, 44. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00259-1
title: The hidden talents approach: adversity enhances some social and cognitive abilities
description: The hidden talents approach is a framework, rooted in biology, psychology, and anthropology, holding that some abilities developed under adversity are strengths rather than deficits. The editorial describes how Muskens et al. "adopted a hidden talents approach" to theorize that "some social and cognitive abilities are enhanced, rather than impaired, through adversity", such as detecting threats, finding creative solutions in scarcity, and reading others' intentions. It underpins the editorial's argument that low-SES children's attributes are specialized skills often underappreciated in academic contexts, not deficiencies to fix.
requirements: Academic contexts must recognize and value the specialized skills developed under adversity for the approach to inform intervention design.
constraints: The editorial notes the approach's prediction about real-world math items was contradicted in the TIMSS analysis it reports.
target_learners: children from low-SES backgrounds
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
accurate recognition of low-SES students' strengths
examples: Muskens et al. used the approach to hypothesize low-SES students would perform better on math items about money, food, and social relationships; the hypothesis was not supported.

article_title: Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status
citation: Marjolein Muskens, Willem E. Frankenhuiss & Lex Borghans. (2024). Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00228-8
title: The hidden talents approach: adversity may enhance rather than impair specific cognitive abilities
description: The hidden talents approach "proposes that adaptive developmental processes might result in certain cognitive abilities being enhanced, rather than impaired, by adversity". A general pattern in prior studies is that performance of people living in poverty or adversity "bene ﬁts more from ecologically relevant materials than the performance of people from more favorable environments does", including working-memory tasks where achievement gaps nearly closed with ecologically relevant content. The article notes evidence for most hidden talents is currently mixed, and this study's results were unexpected from this approach.
requirements: Prior studies supporting the approach focused on executive-function components developed in home environments without formal schooling.
constraints: The article states evidence for most hidden talents is currently limited and mixed; the approach did not predict this study's test-performance findings.
target_learners: children and youth living in poverty or adverse conditions
target_learning_goals: understanding how adversity shapes cognitive abilities relevant to assessment and instruction
examples: The article cites executive-functioning studies where youth exposed to poverty and violence scored lower on abstract working-memory updating tasks but the gap nearly closed with ecologically relevant content, and market-selling studies showing math abilities untapped by formal tests.

article_title: A visual generalization gradient of conceptual stimuli based on fear acquisition in visual and auditory modalities
citation: Xin Liu, Benjamin Becker, Ya Jie Wang, Ying Mei, Haoran Dou & Yi Lei. (2025). A visual generalization gradient of conceptual stimuli based on fear acquisition in visual and auditory modalities. npj Science of Learning 10:37. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00318-1
title: Hierarchical network model of conceptual fear generalization
description: The article invokes the hierarchical network model to explain why conceptually similar stimuli elicit stronger generalized fear. Concepts are "stored as nodes within a network, with connections to other related concepts (e.g., orioles, ﬁsh) varying by similarity and relevance". During concept processing a distance effect emerges: greater conceptual distance makes categorization and generalization harder, so stimuli with higher conceptual similarity are perceived as analogous threat sources and elicit stronger fear responses. The authors state their gradient findings support this framework for crossmodal fear generalization.
requirements: Stimuli must share conceptual (not merely perceptual) similarity with the conditioned stimulus for the network-distance account to apply
constraints: The article presents the model as an interpretive framework supported by its gradient findings, not as a directly tested mechanism; fNIRS could not distinguish prelimbic and infralimbic mPFC functions
target_learners: adult learners in laboratory fear-conditioning studies
individuals with anxiety-related disorders (as discussed by the authors)
target_learning_goals: understanding how learned threat responses generalize across conceptually related stimuli
examples: The study's GSs were drawn from conceptual categories related to the sparrow CS+ (e.g., Pigeon as GS1, Duck as GS2, Goat as GS3), with fear responses weakening as conceptual distance increased

article_title: The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor
citation: Christa Cody, Mehak Maniktala, Nicholas Lytle, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2021). The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05741
title: Hint Factory: data-driven Next-Step hint generation via Markov Decision Process
description: The Hint Factory is a data-driven method for generating hints by transforming historical student problem-solving attempts into a Markov Decision Process, using observed frequencies as transition probabilities. It estimates the expected value of each previously-observed problem state by "assigning rewards to complete solutions, small negative rewards (i.e. costs) to steps to positively reward more eﬃcient solutions, and large negative rewards to errors." Individual student attempts are represented as states with transitions when students add or delete nodes or make errors. The method selects a target state with the highest expected value and uses the latest statement derived there as a pointing hint.
requirements: Historical student data from prior correct solutions to the same problem, combined into an interaction network
constraints: Requires well-defined domains with multiple valid solutions; the process can be done offline with a simple table for real-time hint provision
target_learners: undergraduate students in a discrete mathematics course

description: The article interprets its findings through instructional design frameworks such as 4C/ID, arguing that "the additional hints in the feedback messages served as supportive information during practice, which is particularly effective for novice learners who are still acquiring schemata". examples: In the experiment, students in the MCR + H condition received one hint after a first incorrect answer, e.g., a note explaining how the estimated variance fits into the formula for calculating the standard deviation

article_title: Bridging the Evidence Gap in Developmental Education
citation: Collins, M. L. (2010). Bridging the Evidence Gap in Developmental Education. Journal of Developmental Education, 34(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=%22Bridging+the+Evidence+Gap+in+Developmental+Education%22
title: Hierarchy of research evidence in developmental education: experimental, quasiexperimental, nonexperimental, and descriptive designs ranked by rigor
description: The article describes a hierarchy of evidence, defined largely by quantitative researchers, in which "experimental research designs featuring random assignment are considered the most rigorous, followed by quasiexperimental and nonexperimental research designs; descriptive research is considered the least rigorous methodology." Experimental designs assign a matched experimental group and control group so outcome differences are attributed to the intervention. Quasiexperimental designs, notably regression-discontinuity studies using placement cut scores, apply similar statistical controls without random assignment. The article uses this hierarchy to explain why practitioner-oriented and quantitatively-oriented researchers reach opposing conclusions.
requirements: Understanding of each design type's comparison groups, statistical controls, and selection-bias handling as the article defines them
constraints: The article argues the hierarchy is defensible statistically but does not acknowledge the context of community colleges or the several types of evidence leaders can use
target_learners: academically underprepared community college students
target_learning_goals: identifying effective developmental education programs and practices
examples: Regression-discontinuity studies rely on placement assessment cut scores so that students just below and just above the cut serve as comparison groups

article_title: Teaching High-Value Pronunciation Features: Contrastive Stress for Intermediate Learners
citation: John M. Levis & Greta Muller Levis. (2018). Teaching High-Value Pronunciation Features: Contrastive Stress for Intermediate Learners. The CATESOL Journal, 30(1). https://www.catesoljournal.org
title: High-value pronunciation features and the intelligibility-based triage approach to pronunciation teaching
description: The article frames pronunciation teaching around identifying high-value features: those whose improvement most affects how listeners process and rate speech. "By high value, we mean that changes in the feature, even if everything else remains the same, are likely to make listeners rate speech more positively than if the feature is not correctly used." Gilbert's analogy to medical triage underlies this intelligibility-based approach, in which more important features are addressed before less important ones. The study tests contrastive stress as a candidate high-value feature for comprehensibility.
requirements: Identifying which features affect listener processing requires evidence about listener ratings rather than accuracy alone
constraints: The article notes that learnability assertions in pronunciation teaching often have little evidence beyond teacher experience, and that improvement in controlled contexts may not transfer to free speech
target_learners: L2 learners of English, including intermediate ESL learners
target_learning_goals: improving comprehensibility of L2 speech
examples: The study isolated contrastive stress by requiring it in the picture-comparison answers, allowing the authors to examine its contribution to comprehensibility

title: HITCOMP framework: a five-domain health information technology competency taxonomy used as the study's sensitising framework
description: The Health Information Technology Competencies (HITCOMP) framework is a competency taxonomy for the healthcare workforce. The article states that "The Health Information Technology Competencies (HITCOMP) framework offers five domains: administration, direct patient care, engineering/information systems/ICT, informatics and research/biomedicine." In this study, HITCOMP's administrative-interaction quadrant served as a sensitising concept for the interview guide, and administrators selected competencies pertinent to their roles from it. The article also judges HITCOMP a suitable fit for postgraduate healthcare management curricula, capacity-building programmes and short-term certifications due to its modular nature.
requirements: Contextual mapping for settings with limited resources, infrastructure difficulties or regional disparities in digital literacy
constraints: HITCOMP does not automatically take into consideration situations with limited resources, infrastructure difficulties or regional disparities in digital literacy, per the article's Indian contextual gap analysis

postgraduate healthcare management students
target_learning_goals: Health information technology competencies for administrative interactions
digital competency development across care levels
examples: Respondents selected competencies from the administrative interaction quadrant of the administration domain of the HITCOMP framework during interviews

article_title: Navigating hidden barriers in clinical medical education in Iran: a qualitative study.
citation: Hazrati Hakimeh, Rezazadeh Khatereh, Barzegar Mohammad. (2025). Navigating hidden barriers in clinical medical education in Iran: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08120-8
title: Three-theme framework of hidden barriers in Iranian clinical medical education
description: The article organizes its qualitative findings into a framework of three overarching themes: (1) ineffective management of clinical education, (2) limited focus on training socially responsive physicians, and (3) shifts in professional perspectives in medicine. Each theme contains categories and subcategories derived from interview data. The authors interpret the themes "with reference to competency-based medical education (CBME), social accountability frameworks, and cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT), alongside classic learning theories."

constraints: Findings reflect the Iranian centralized higher-education context integrating medical education with healthcare service delivery

clinical faculty members
target_learning_goals: clinical competence
professional identity and social accountability
examples: The theme of ineffective management includes categories such as limited resources, incoherent planning, poor education-service integration, and selection mechanisms misaligned with educational goals.

citation: Iwabuchi Serena, Okata Yuichi, Kameoka Yasuyuki, Miyauchi Harunori, Yoshimura Shohei, Komyo Yuki, Kajihara Keisuke, Nakai Yumiko, Bitoh Yuko. (2025). Initial adaptation and surgical performance of the hinotori™ robotic system among pediatric surgeons with minimal robotic exposure. Pediatric Surgery International. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00383-025-06212-6
title: hinotori™ Surgical Robot System with A-Lap Mini assessment in a simulated infant abdomen
description: The hinotori™ Surgical Robot System (Medicaroid Inc., Kobe, Japan) comprises "a master console and three robotic arms equipped with a 10-mm, 30° videoscope and two 8-mm ports", with eight-axis arms and a docking-free architecture enabling compact port placement. In this study it was evaluated against conventional 5-mm laparoscopic instruments in a 1,400-mL transparent acrylic training box (Endowork Pro II) simulating the abdominal cavity of a 6-month-old infant, with suturing accuracy automatically quantified by the A-Lap Mini computer-assisted device across five scored components (maximum total 25).

target_learning_goals: Laparoscopic and robotic suturing and peg-transfer skills in confined pediatric-like operative spaces
examples: Ten pediatric surgeons performed peg transfer of six triangular blocks on a 12-peg board and three single-knot sutures on a four-layer artificial intestinal model, with order of approaches randomized

citation: Yang Ziqing, Zhen Siyu, Pan Ben, Wei Hanyu, Li Qiang, Yue Junyan, Hu Ying, Liang Changhua. (2025). Investigating the use of the HIS-based BOPPPS teaching model in medical imaging experimental course instruction. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07607-8
title: HIS-based BOPPPS implementation for the medical imaging experimental course (crossover design, 117 interns)
description: An instructional implementation in which 117 medical imaging interns at the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinxiang Medical University (2021–2022 academic year) were taught in two groups across two semesters in a crossover design: the first group used the HIS-based BOPPPS model in semester one while the second used traditional teaching, and the models were swapped in semester two "to eliminate potential inter-group difference impacts on the results." clinical thinking

description: Peer-led teaching sessions supplement conventional teaching by having students who have attained curriculum milestones teach other students in the same program. At Kirk Kerkorian School of Medicine, "High-Yield Review sessions, equivalent to PLTS, involve second-year students teaching high-yield content on specific topics."
