title: Focus on high-quality onboarding programmes to close the experience-related quality gap in stroke thrombolysis
description: Because less experienced registrars had longer door-to-needle times, the article recommends investing in onboarding to compensate for experience gained only through treating real patients. It states: "We suggest a focus on high-quality onboarding programmes to close the experience-related quality gap." The authors note that with high physician turnover, a larger proportion of patients are treated by less experienced registrars, negatively affecting DNT, and that simulation plus systemic changes produced larger gains than experience alone.
requirements: Onboarding that compensates for the DNT advantage accumulated through real-life case experience
constraints: Even a difference of minutes affects patient outcomes, so the gap is clinically meaningful; local onboarding procedures shape the findings
target_learners: newly hired neurology registrars in acute stroke care
target_learning_goals: reducing door-to-needle time in intravenous thrombolysis
examples: New registrars at the study hospital receive a 1-day introductory course on acute stroke care followed by a 2-week training period

title: High-fidelity trauma panscan simulation program with four escalating cases and a hot-seat group session
description: A simulation training program for PGY-3 radiology residents before overnight call, built from four simulation panscans combining real CT studies from different patients to depict multi-system traumatic injuries, displayed as scrollable Powerpoint files simulating the CT console. Individual sessions escalate across four cases with decreasing review time (12, 10, 7 min) and rising pressure, including a senior resident role-playing a "belligerent and pressured surgery resident" and hospital noise audio, followed by feedback and a joint radiology–surgery group discussion. A later 1.5-h group session uses the "hot seat" format with Socratic questioning.
requirements: A senior radiology resident and one or two radiology attendings present for the entire training session
Simulation panscans showing only axial images at scanner slice thickness with scanner window/levels and reconstruction order
A group training session with attending emergency radiology, trauma surgeon, and neurosurgeon discussion
constraints: Training was delivered individually to second-year residents prior to the start of overnight on-call duties at a single academic level 1 trauma center
target_learners: PGY-3 radiology residents
2nd and 3rd year radiology residents in the group session
target_learning_goals: Identify injuries requiring immediate surgical attention at the CT scanner
Communicate findings concisely and decisively to trauma surgeons under pressure
examples: Case 4 ended with surgeons providing "loud, vigorous, and authentic clinical simulation of a severely traumatic patient" and rushing the patient from the scanner to the operating room

article_title: HipSim - hip fracture surgery simulation utilizing the Learning Curve-Cumulative Summation test (LC-CUSUM).
citation: Rölfing Jan Duedal, Jensen Rune Dall, Paltved Charlotte. (2020). HipSim — hip fracture surgery simulation utilizing the Learning Curve–Cumulative Summation test (LC-CUSUM). Acta Orthopaedica 91(6): 669–674. https://doi.org/10.1080/17453674.2020.1777511
title: HipSim — a stepwise mastery-learning VR simulation program for the dynamic hip screw procedure with LC-CUSUM-based advancement
description: HipSim is a virtual reality dynamic hip screw (DHS) training program on the TraumaVision simulator, designed as 'a time-dispersed mastery-learning program with 2–3 training days of a maximum 4 hours of training per day'. Participants advance stepwise through three competency levels, from repetitive K-wire placement in the same patient to the entire DHS procedure, with clinical variability of 'up to 24 different scenarios (different patients and fracture patterns)' introduced at CL1.
requirements: Participants must be 1st-year orthopedic residents who have performed fewer than 10 hip fracture-related surgeries under supervision.
Advancement to the next competency level is granted only when LC-CUSUM signals competency; a minimum of 39 procedures was required to complete all 3 CLs, with a maximum of 50 procedures per level.
constraints: The article states VR simulation is 'currently neither suited to teaching the participants the entire procedure including reposition of the fracture and soft-tissue handling nor does it encompass the overwhelming complexity of performing the procedure in the operating theatre'.

The article states the results of HipSim 'should not and cannot be used as a summative assessment of the participant's capabilities to become a competent surgeon'; it is a formative program with summative evaluation of each simulation.
target_learners: 1st-year orthopedic residents with fewer than 10 hip fracture surgeries
target_learning_goals: mastering the dynamic hip screw procedure
hand–eye coordination and working in 3 dimensions from 2-dimensional visual information with haptic feedback
examples: 32 1st-year residents trained across CL0–CL2; 14 reached an LC-CUSUM score of 39 and passed, with a maximum of 50 simulations at each of the 3 CLs to obtain a score of 13 and advance.

Cases from multiple categories mixed within a study session
constraints: Preliminary testing showed learners prefer shorter decks with fewer than 30 cards, though larger decks may produce more spacing

durable memory

title: Multi-component HIV and AIDS programme design combining case studies, accredited training, clinical competencies, mentorship, repeated skills-practice sessions and a dedicated resource room

citation: Casper Anne M., Eddy Sarah L., Freeman Scott. (2019). True Grit: Passion and persistence make an innovative course design work. PLoS Biology. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000359
title: High-structure course design: preclass preparation, in-class active learning, and postclass self-testing bracketing intensive active learning
description: A course design in which students "learn basic content on their own prior to class, with a quiz based on assigned readings or videos," apply content to higher-order problems through peer-based active-learning exercises during class with instructor feedback, and test understanding after class with a low-stakes quiz or practice exam. requirements: Students prepare basic content before class via quiz-incentivized readings or videos
In-class time is devoted to higher-order active-learning exercises with peers and instructor feedback

target_learning_goals: introductory biology content: biological molecules, cell structure and function, energetics, cell division, genetics, evolution, and ecology
examples: Experiment 3 combined 15-minute instructor video lectures with closed-notes peer-graded prep quizzes, group worksheets, peer-instruction clicker questions, random call, and weekly untimed online practice exams of 20–30 questions

title: Hidden curriculum and secondary socialization framework for medical students' professional identity formation
description: The article frames medical education as participation in a community of practice where professional identity forms through explicit, informal, and hidden curricula. Identity is shaped "even more by each individual's largely unconscious internalizations of the behaviors, language, and conceptions of knowledge and quality inherent in medical teaching." Secondary socialization transforms lay youths into professionals through tacit adaptation whereby newcomers relinquish aspects of their former selves and adopt the norms dominating their new environment.
requirements: Participation over years in a community where trainees interact with peers, teachers, patients, and medical role models
constraints: The study reports no direct data on informants' mental health; socialization mechanisms are inferred from discourse
target_learners: first-year medical students in a traditional preclinical curriculum

article_title: Improving Exam Performance in Introductory Biology through the Use of Preclass Reading Guides.
citation: Lieu, R., Wong, A., Asefirad, A., & Shaffer, J. F. (2017). Improving Exam Performance in Introductory Biology through the Use of Preclass Reading Guides. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5589426/
title: High-structure course design requiring preclass content acquisition paired with in-class active learning
description: The article situates reading guides within high-structure (and flipped) course designs, in which "students acquire content before class and then perform active-learning exercises in class" or complete graded preclass and weekly review assignments. The instructor-designed reading guides serve the preclass content-acquisition role in this structure, freeing class time for clicker questions, group work, discussion, and formative testing of misconceptions.
requirements: Course content must be deliverable outside class time, via textbook reading or videos
Some guidance and/or reward for completing preclass reading, which prior studies identified as common themes
constraints: Not reading before class "may be a recipe for disaster" in flipped or high-structure courses where preclass preparation is critical
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large-enrollment college biology courses
target_learning_goals: Active engagement with course content before class so class time can be used for active learning and scientific literacy skills
examples: The studied course required daily preclass Mastering Biology assignments, in-class clicker questions and group work, and weekly review quizzes, with reading guides supporting the reading component
